# Lead and sub-team agent profiles: structuring an agent org that delegates without losing the plot

When you give one agent everything, it forgets the goal halfway through. When you give ten agents a shared chat, they talk past each other and quietly drift. The middle path is a small org of named profiles, each with a bounded remit, and a lead agent that holds the plot while specialists do the work. This is a log of how I structured one, what broke, and what I would do differently.

## The problem with flat agent orgs

Most agent setups I have seen fall into one of two failure modes. The first is the monolith: a single agent with a long system prompt, a fat tool list, and a vague instruction to "do the task". It works for a demo and then degrades. The context window fills, earlier instructions get softened by later ones, and the agent starts optimising for whatever was said most recently rather than what mattered most.

The second is the swarm: many agents in a shared channel, each with a slice of capability, all able to message each other. This looks modern and feels productive. In practice it is expensive, hard to debug, and nobody is responsible for the goal. You get a lot of activity and very little accountability. When something goes wrong you cannot tell which profile made the call that broke the build.

The durable pattern that fixes both is not a tool. It is an operating model: a small number of profiles with explicit remits, one of which is the lead, and a document that says what each one is for. The economics matter. A lead agent that only plans and delegates is cheap to run because its context stays small. Specialists are expensive but short-lived, spun up for a unit of work and torn down. The cost per task drops because you are not paying a monolith to re-read its own history on every turn.

## The mechanism: profiles as bounded contexts

The idea I borrowed is older than agents. In domain-driven design you draw a bounded context around a subsystem so that words mean one thing inside it and do not leak out. For agents, a profile is a bounded context for behaviour. It has a name, a remit, a tool list, a memory scope, and a policy. Anything outside the remit is explicitly not its problem.

A profile is not just a system prompt. A system prompt is what you say to the model. A profile is the full envelope: the prompt, the tools it is allowed to call, the files it is allowed to read, the other profiles it is allowed to hand off to, and the policies it must satisfy before it returns. The prompt is the smallest part. The boundaries are the part that keeps the plot.

I keep two documents at the centre. One is a North Star: a short statement of the goal the whole org serves, written so any profile can read it in a few seconds and re-anchor. The other is a multi-profile operating model: a table of profiles, their remits, their handoff rules, and their acceptance criteria. These are plain text. They are not clever. They are the cheapest coherence mechanism I have found.

## Worked example: a lead and two specialists

Here is the shape I actually ran. Three profiles, one lead.

The lead agent, call it the coordinator, has a narrow job. It reads the task, breaks it into units, assigns each unit to a specialist, waits for results, checks them against acceptance criteria, and either accepts or sends back with a specific fix request. It does not write code. It does not run tools beyond a handoff tool and a check tool. Its context stays small because it never does the work itself.

```text
profile: coordinator
remit: decompose, delegate, verify
tools: handoff, check
memory: North Star, operating model, current task state
policy: never execute specialist work; never accept without check
```

The first specialist is a builder. It receives a unit with a clear scope, does the work, runs the relevant tests, and returns a diff plus evidence. It cannot see the North Star directly. It sees the slice the coordinator passes it. This is deliberate. If the builder could read everything it would start optimising for the whole goal and drift.

```text
profile: builder
remit: implement one unit, run tests, return diff
tools: edit, test, search
memory: unit brief, relevant files
policy: do not start work without a unit brief; do not return without green tests
```

The second specialist is a reviewer. It takes a diff and a unit brief, checks the diff against the brief and against the codebase conventions, and returns a verdict with specific notes. It cannot edit. This separation sounds wasteful but it is the thing that stops the builder from marking its own homework.

```text
profile: reviewer
remit: verify diff against brief and conventions
tools: read, search
memory: diff, unit brief, conventions
policy: no edits; verdict must cite specific lines
```

The handoff is the interesting part. The coordinator does not say "go do the task". It passes a structured unit: the goal slice, the files in scope, the acceptance criteria, and a deadline in turns. The specialist returns a structured result: what it did, what it tested, what it could not do, and what it needs next. Nothing is free-text chat. Everything is a typed handoff. This is what keeps the lead from losing the plot. The lead never has to read a paragraph and decide what the specialist meant.

## Policy enforcement as the immune system

Profiles and handoffs get you structure. They do not get you safety. A builder can still ship a broken diff if its tests are wrong. A reviewer can still rubber-stamp if its conventions doc is thin. The pattern I found useful, drawn from runtime security work on autonomous agents, is to treat policy as a three-layer immune system that runs inside the agent loop rather than as a perimeter around it.

The first layer is detection. Before a specialist returns, it must self-check against its policy. "Run tests before returning" is a detection rule. The second layer is containment. If the check fails, the specialist cannot hand back. It must either fix or escalate. The third layer is recovery. If the coordinator sees a failed handback, it rewrites the unit brief and re-delegates. It does not let the broken result propagate.

The key insight is that tool-call interception is not enough. A policy that says "do not commit without tests" is useless if the agent commits through a path your interceptor does not see. The durable fix is to push the policy down to the execution layer so that the commit command itself refuses to run without evidence. In practice, for a small org, this means your check tool is not a polite request. It is a gate the specialist cannot route around. You wire the gate into the harness, not into the prompt.

## Trade-offs: cost, latency, and coherence

The win is coherence. The coordinator's context stays clean, so it keeps the goal in view across many units. The specialists are replaceable, so you can swap a builder for a better one without retraining the org. The cost is latency and tokens. Every handoff is a round trip. A task a monolith does in one shot takes three or four turns here.

The trade-off I keep revisiting is how much the coordinator should see. Give it too little and it accepts work it should have rejected. Give it too much and you are back to a monolith with extra steps. The rule I settled on: the coordinator sees the verdict, not the diff. It trusts the reviewer's structured verdict and only reads the diff when the verdict is contested. This keeps its context under a page most of the time.

The other trade-off is profile count. Three profiles is the sweet spot for me. Five starts to feel like a swarm. Two collapses back into a monolith with a helper. The number is not magic. It follows from how many distinct remits you can write down without overlap. If two profiles have overlapping remits, merge them. Overlap is where the plot gets lost.

## Reality check: hype versus practice

The hype says multi-agent orgs are autonomous and self-organising. The practice is that you write the org chart yourself and you maintain it. Profiles do not discover their remits. You define them, test them, and fix them when they drift. The "self-organising" framing is mostly wishful. What you actually get is a set of contracts you enforce by hand until the harness is solid.

The harder-than-it-looks part is the acceptance criteria. A profile is only as good as the check that gates its output. Writing "the tests pass" is easy. Writing "the diff actually addresses the unit brief and does not introduce regressions in adjacent modules" is real engineering. I spent more time on check rules than on any prompt.

Policy enforcement is also oversold. The immune system pattern is sound, but in practice the recovery layer is where everything falls down. Detection and containment are mechanical. Recovery requires the coordinator to understand why a specialist failed and rewrite the brief. That is a reasoning task, not a rule. It fails on edge cases and you end up handling them yourself. Plan for that. Do not pretend the org is closed-loop when it is actually a loop with a human in the gap.

## How to apply this

1. Write a one-page North Star. State the goal in a way any profile can re-read in seconds. If it is longer than a page, it is not a North Star, it is a spec.
2. List the remits you actually need. Start with three: a coordinator, a builder, a reviewer. Only add a fourth when you can write its remit without overlapping the first three.
3. Define the handoff format. Use structured units and structured results. Ban free-text chat between profiles. This is the single highest-leverage decision.
4. Wire the check as a gate, not a suggestion. The specialist cannot return without evidence. The coordinator cannot accept without a verdict.
5. Keep the coordinator's context small. It sees verdicts, not diffs. It re-reads the North Star every turn. It never does specialist work, even when that would be faster.
6. Run a smoke test of the whole org on a small task before trusting it on a real one. Watch where the handoff format is ambiguous and fix the format, not the prompt.

## What I'd try next

I want to make the coordinator cheaper by giving it a cached view of the operating model so it does not re-read the table every turn. I also want to try a fourth profile, a planner that sits between the coordinator and the specialists and owns the decomposition, so the coordinator becomes purely a verifier. The risk is that I add a layer and lose the simplicity that makes this work. Before I build it, I will write the remit on a postcard. If it does not fit, the profile does not exist yet.
